name: spin
desc: Efficient verification tool of multi-threaded software
why: Model checker that explores every interleaving of a concurrent protocol, a window into how distributed bugs are found.

brief.what_it_is: Spin is an open-source software verification tool for formal verification of multi-threaded software applications. You write a model of a concurrent system in its modelling language (the example uses a .pml file), and Spin checks it against assertions and properties. The homepage's example models Peterson's mutual exclusion algorithm with two processes and an assertion that only one is in the critical section, then runs it with spin -run. The page does not say explicitly what output Spin produces beyond the pass or fail result of its checks.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Spin as a tool for formal verification of multi-threaded software, developed at Bell Labs starting in 1980 and freely available since 1991. It also notes that Spin won the ACM System Software Award in April 2002.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal mechanism. Its example shows a model built from shared variables and active processes (proctype), with assertions and a goto loop, and the page mentions an automata-theoretic verification method in its course material.

commands_seen.context: Shown as the analysis step for the Peterson's mutual exclusion example model on the homepage; runs Spin on the model file peterson.pml.

brief.install_notes: Nothing about installation appears on the homepage. A separate installation page is linked from the site navigation but was not fetched. The brew entry gives only the executable name spin.
brief.standout: Spin has a long history, dating to 1980 at Bell Labs, and the homepage pitches it as a verifier for concurrent and multi-threaded code rather than only for hardware. Its sources moved to the BSD 3-Clause license in January 2016, and the site lists a free online course and a semester-long course built around it.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage says the current version is 6.5.1 (July 2020), so the most recent release it names is about six years old. The site is still updated, with a 2026 symposium announcement, and it says Spin 'continues to evolve', so it is not abandoned. The page does not give a commit date.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not say that Spin explores every interleaving, which is the scout note's claim; that is the usual model-checking idea but was not confirmed here. The page does not describe platforms, build requirements, or limits on model size. Parts of the course material are behind a password. The homepage also advertises an unrelated tool, Cobra, which is not part of Spin.

entry.title: Spin
entry.tldr: Spin checks models of concurrent programs against assertions, so you can test a mutual exclusion algorithm like Peterson's before it ever runs as real code.
entry.deeper_look:
Spin is a verification tool for multi-threaded software. You do not point it at your code directly. You write a model of the system in its own modelling language, usually in a .pml file, and Spin checks that model against the assertions and properties you state. The homepage's example models Peterson's mutual exclusion algorithm: two processes, some shared variables, a goto loop, and an assertion that only one process is ever in the critical section.

Spin began at Bell Labs in 1980 and has been freely available since 1991. It won the ACM System Software Award in April 2002. Its sources moved to the BSD 3-Clause license in January 2016. The homepage says it "continues to evolve to keep pace with new developments in the field."

The idea underneath is formal verification of concurrency. Concurrent bugs tend to hide in rare orderings of events that testing seldom hits. A model checker works on a description of the system instead of a lucky run. The homepage mentions an automata-theoretic verification method in its course material, but it does not explain the internals, so treat the details as something to read up on after you have run the first example.

The homepage also lists a free online course and a semester-long course built around Spin, which makes it a reasonable entry point into the field.

try_this.what_happens: Runs Spin's analysis on the homepage's Peterson's mutual exclusion model and reports whether the assertion holds. You write peterson.pml yourself from the example on the homepage.
Prints the list of Spin's command-line options.

entry.whats_unique: It has been around since 1980 and is aimed at concurrent and multi-threaded software rather than hardware. You describe the algorithm in a small modelling language and have it checked, instead of testing real code.
entry.caveats: The latest release the homepage names is 6.5.1 from July 2020, and the page says nothing about platforms, build requirements, or limits on model size. Some course material is password-protected.
